1. The animation shows that paying extra principal on a mortgage has a guaranteed return equal to the loan's own rate. For Tessa's 30-year loan that is 7.40% a year, before taxes. This is interest she no longer pays, not an investment return. The 7.40% works as a bar that any other use of the money has to clear.

2. A dollar bill starts beside Tessa's house, then moves up onto a platform at the 7.40% level, measured against a zero line. The label "interest no longer charged" appears next. In the last two frames a dashed, faded bill labeled "any other use" appears next to the bar. The final label reads "not tested."

3. It means that putting extra money into the mortgage saves interest at the loan's rate. That rate is the benchmark for comparing alternatives. The video does not say whether any investment beats 7.40%. It leaves that question open, noting that risk and taxes would matter.

4. The video gives no instruction. A viewer could take away a way to frame the choice: compare the loan's rate to what another use of the money might earn after risk and taxes. That is a framing, not a recommendation to prepay or to invest.

5. None. The video gave no advice, so there is nothing to attribute. Its narration and on-screen text explicitly say the comparison "isn't tested here."
